name: Default Effect
description: The pre-selected option in a choice is disproportionately likely to be chosen, independent of its objective merits.
design_relevance_note: The single most consistently effective, ethically defensible nudge technique in the entire corpus — pre-checked settings, opt-out vs. opt-in flows.
myth_risk_note: Default effects are well-established for binary/discrete choices but the literature search found limited evidence testing robustness across domains or examining when defaults fail. The narrow empirical base relative to popularity suggests some caution, though no explicit failed replications appear.
prevalence_note: The most commonly cited choice-architecture lever in practice — opt-in vs. opt-out framing is a standard design-review discussion point.

findings.description: Across 58 default studies (pooled n = 73,675), pre-selected options raised selection with a considerable average effect (d = 0.68, 95% CI 0.53-0.83) but with substantial variation: most studies found positive effects, several found none, and two found negative effects. Defaults were more effective in consumer domains and less effective in environmental ones, and more effective when seen as endorsement or as reflecting the status quo (endowment).
findings.source_title: When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects

findings.description: Default policy design (opt-in vs. opt-out) produces large, consistent differences in real-world organ donation consent rates across countries, demonstrated via cross-national data plus a dedicated experiment.
findings.effect_size: Large cross-country differences in donation rates (opt-out vs. opt-in regimes)

applications.title: Setting the default electricity contract to 'green' energy so customers must actively opt out
applications.description: In a randomized controlled trial in Germany, the default choice was set to more expensive 'green' energy contracts made entirely from renewable sources, so that consumers had to opt out if they did not want it. Purchases of green energy were compared with the version where customers had to opt in. Follow-up experiments probed whether the effect came from customers being unaware of the default. The energy provider is not named in the abstract and is not named here.
applications.ethical_note: The default pushes customers toward a more expensive product, which serves the environmental aim and, for many, their stated values, but means some people end up paying more without having actively chosen to. The paper's follow-up experiments found the effect did not seem to be driven by unawareness, which weakens the worry that people were simply unaware of what they bought, though it does not show everyone endorsed the extra cost. Opting out stayed possible, which keeps the choice open.

applications.title: Square's payment terminal defaulting to a 'tipping' state
applications.description: Square's mobile-payment app/terminal sets its checkout screen to a default 'tipping' state, requiring the customer to actively select a 'no tipping' option if they don't want to leave a tip -- reported to raise tip amounts, especially in contexts (like counter service) where tipping had not previously been customary.
applications.ethical_note: The 'guilts you into leaving tips' framing in the very article this claim traces back to signals a real manipulative dimension -- the default exploits social discomfort with actively opting out in front of the person being tipped (or their POS system), a dynamic distinct from a default that merely saves the user effort on a decision they're indifferent to.
